items.prose: A broker checks 40 client accounts against a rule: **if an account's leverage is over 5, it was sent a margin call**. Of the 40, 12 have leverage over 5, 15 were sent a margin call, and 9 are in both groups.

parts.question: How many accounts have leverage over 5 but were not sent a margin call?

feedback.correct: Of the 12 accounts with leverage over 5, 9 got a call, so $12 - 9 = 3$ did not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from the 12 accounts with leverage over 5 and take away those that got a call.

byKey.swapped: That is the accounts with a call but leverage of 5 or less, $15 - 9$. Start from the 12 with leverage over 5.
byKey.both: 9 accounts have both. Take them away from the 12 with leverage over 5: $12 - 9 = 3$.

explain.text: An account breaks the rule only when its leverage is over 5 and no call was sent. Of the 12 with leverage over 5, 9 got a call, so $12 - 9 = 3$ did not.

parts.question: Using 3 from part 1, on how many of the 40 accounts is the rule true?

feedback.correct: The rule fails only on the 3 accounts with leverage over 5 and no call, so it holds on $40 - 3 = 37$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where an implication is false, then count the rest.

byKey.true-true: You counted only the accounts where both parts are true. An implication with a false 'if' part is true too. So the 28 accounts with leverage of 5 or less also keep the rule.
byKey.breakers: 3 is the number of accounts that break the rule. The question asks where it holds: $40 - 3 = 37$.

explain.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, which is 3 accounts. So the rule is true on the other $40 - 3 = 37$. That includes the 28 accounts with leverage of 5 or less, whose 'if' part is false.

parts.question: The converse reads: **if an account was sent a margin call, its leverage is over 5**. On how many of the 40 accounts is the converse false?

feedback.correct: The converse fails when a call was sent and leverage is 5 or less: $15 - 9 = 6$ accounts.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The converse swaps the parts. Find where its 'if' part is true and its 'then' part false.

byKey.rule: 3 is where the original rule fails. The converse fails when a call was sent but leverage is 5 or less: $15 - 9 = 6$.
byKey.true-count: 34 is where the converse holds. The question asks where it fails: $15 - 9 = 6$.

explain.text: $Q \Rightarrow P$ is false when $Q$ is true and $P$ is false. Of the 15 calls, 9 went to accounts with leverage over 5, so $15 - 9 = 6$ accounts break the converse. A rule and its converse fail on different accounts.

parts.question: The broker's report says: **every account keeps the rule**. Which sentence is the negation of the report?

options.text: There is an account with leverage over 5 that was not sent a margin call
Every account with leverage over 5 was not sent a margin call at all
options.why: You negated the 'then' part but kept 'every'. One account that breaks the rule is enough to deny the report.

options.text: There is an account that was sent a margin call with leverage of 5 or less
options.why: That account breaks the converse, not the rule. The rule says nothing about accounts with leverage of 5 or less.

options.text: If an account's leverage is over 5, then it was not sent a margin call
options.why: You negated only the 'then' part and kept the 'if'. The negation of an implication is an 'and': $P$ and not $Q$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot \forall a\,(P \Rightarrow Q)$ is $\exists a\,(P \land \lnot Q)$, and part 1 found 3 such accounts.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn 'every' into 'there is', then negate the implication inside.

explain.text: The report is $\forall a\,(P \Rightarrow Q)$, so its negation is $\exists a\,(P \land \lnot Q)$: an account with leverage over 5 and no call. Part 1 found 3 of them, so the report is false.

items.prose: A trading script reads three statements each morning. $P$: yesterday's close was above its 20-day average. $Q$: yesterday's volume was above 3 million shares. $R$: the bid-ask spread is wider than 4 pence. The script buys when $(P \lor Q) \land \lnot R$ is true.

parts.question: On Monday the close was £8.40 against an average of £8.25. Volume was 2.6 million shares and the spread was 5 pence. How many of $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are true on Monday?

feedback.correct: $P$ is true ($8.40 > 8.25$), $Q$ is false (2.6 million is not above 3 million) and $R$ is true ($5 > 4$). That makes 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test each statement against Monday's figures on its own.

byKey.all: Check $Q$: volume of 2.6 million shares is not above 3 million, so $Q$ is false. Only 2 are true.
byKey.one: Check $R$: a spread of 5 pence is wider than 4 pence, so $R$ is true. With $P$ that makes 2.

explain.text: Each line is a statement, so each has a truth value we can check. $8.40 > 8.25$ makes $P$ true, 2.6 million below 3 million makes $Q$ false, and $5 > 4$ makes $R$ true: 2 are true.

parts.question: With $P$ true, $Q$ false and $R$ true from part 1, does the script buy on Monday?

options.text: No: $P \lor Q$ is true, but $\lnot R$ is false
Yes: $P$ is true, so $P \lor Q$ is true
options.why: You stopped at $P \lor Q$. The 'and' also needs $\lnot R$, and $R$ is true.

options.text: No: $Q$ is false, so $P \lor Q$ is false
options.why: An 'or' needs only one true part. $P$ is true, so $P \lor Q$ is true.

options.text: Yes: $R$ is true, so the last condition holds
options.why: The rule asks for $\lnot R$, not $R$. A wide spread blocks the buy.

feedback.correct: Right. True and false is false, so the script does not buy.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $P \lor Q$ and $\lnot R$ first, then join them with 'and'.

explain.text: $P \lor Q$ is true because $P$ is. $\lnot R$ is false because $R$ is true. True and false is false, so the script does not buy.

parts.question: A truth table in $P$, $Q$ and $R$ has 8 rows. On how many rows is $(P \lor Q) \land \lnot R$ true?

feedback.correct: $P \lor Q$ is true on 6 rows, and $R$ is false on half of those: 3 rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the rows where $P \lor Q$ is true, then keep those with $R$ false.

byKey.or-only: 6 rows have $P \lor Q$ true. The 'and' keeps only those with $R$ false, which is half of them: 3.
byKey.not-r-only: 4 rows have $R$ false. One of them has $P$ and $Q$ both false, so $P \lor Q$ fails there: 3 rows are left.
byKey.and: You read $P \lor Q$ as $P \land Q$. An 'or' is true when either part is, so 3 rows buy.

explain.text: $P \lor Q$ is false only when both are false. So it is true for 3 of the 4 pairs of values of $P$ and $Q$. Each pair appears once with $R$ false, so the rule is true on 3 rows.

parts.question: A risk rule says: **if $P \lor Q$, then $\lnot R$**. Using the same 8 rows, on how many is $(P \lor Q) \Rightarrow \lnot R$ true?

widget.label: Rows where the risk rule holds

feedback.correct: It fails only when $P \lor Q$ is true and $R$ is true: 3 rows. So it holds on $8 - 3 = 5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. An implication is false only when its 'if' part is true and its 'then' part false.

byKey.as-and: 3 counts the rows of the 'and' rule, which are also the rows where the implication fails. An implication is also true when its 'if' part is false, so add those 2 rows: 5.
byKey.only-false-if: 2 is the rows where $P \lor Q$ is false. The implication is also true on the 3 rows where both its parts are true: 5 in all.

explain.text: The implication is false only when $P \lor Q$ is true and $R$ is true, which happens on 3 rows. So it is true on $8 - 3 = 5$. The 2 rows beyond the 'and' rule are those with $P$ and $Q$ both false.

items.prose: Four funds' annual returns over four years, in whole per cent. For a whole number $t$, claim A($t$) says every fund had a year with a return above $t$%. Claim B($t$) says there is a year in which every fund returned above $t$%.

parts.question: Which sentence is the negation of B(5)?

options.text: In every year, at least one fund returned 5% or less
In some year, at least one fund returned 5% or less
options.why: You flipped only the inner 'every'. The outer 'there is a year' must become 'in every year'.

options.text: In every year, every fund returned 5% or less
options.why: You flipped the outer quantifier and kept 'every fund'. Inside, 'every fund' must become 'at least one fund'.

options.text: In every year, at least one fund returned less than 5%
options.why: The negation of 'above 5%' is '5% or less'. A fund at exactly 5% also denies the claim.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot \exists y\ \forall f$ is $\forall y\ \exists f$, with 'above 5%' turned into '5% or less'.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Flip each quantifier in order, then negate 'above 5%' exactly.

explain.text: B(5) is $\exists y\ \forall f$, return above 5%. Its negation is $\forall y\ \exists f$, return of 5% or less. Each quantifier flips, and so does the inequality.

parts.question: How many of the four years are witnesses for B(5)?

feedback.correct: No year works. The lowest returns by year are 2%, 3%, 3% and 1%, all 5% or less.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A witness year needs every fund above 5%, so look at the lowest return in each column.

byKey.some-fund: Every year has some fund above 5%, but B needs every fund above 5% in the same year. The lowest returns by year are 2%, 3%, 3% and 1%, so no year works.

explain.text: A witness year must have all four returns above 5%. The lowest return in each year is 2%, 3%, 3% and 1%, so none is a witness. B(5) is false, as its negation in part 1 says.

parts.question: B(5) is false, but B holds for small $t$. What is the largest whole number $t$ for which B($t$) is true?

feedback.correct: The best year's lowest return is 3%. B($t$) needs that lowest return above $t$, so $t = 2$ is the largest.
feedback.generic: Not quite. For each year find its lowest return, take the largest of those, and stay strictly below it.

byKey.at-least: At $t = 3$ the best year's lowest return is 3%, which is not above 3%. B needs 'above', so the largest $t$ is 2.
byKey.swapped: 6 is the limit for A, where each fund picks its own year. B needs one year shared by every fund, so $t = 2$.

explain.text: B($t$) needs one year whose lowest return is above $t$. The lowest returns by year are 2, 3, 3 and 1, so the best is 3%. B($t$) holds for $t < 3$, and the largest whole $t$ is 2.

parts.question: Using the same table, what is the largest whole number $t$ for which A($t$) is true?

feedback.correct: Each fund's best year is 7%, 8%, 9% and 9%. The weakest of those is 7%, so A($t$) holds for $t < 7$: $t = 6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. For each fund find its best year, take the smallest of those, and stay strictly below it.

byKey.at-least: At $t = 7$ fund F1's best year is 7%, which is not above 7%. So the largest $t$ is 6.
byKey.kept-b: 2 is the limit for B, where one year must serve every fund. In A each fund picks its own year, so the limit is higher: 6.
byKey.best-fund: You used the best fund. Every fund needs a year above $t$, so the weakest fund's best year, 7% for F1, sets the limit: 6.

explain.text: A($t$) lets each fund pick its own year above $t$. The best years are 7, 8, 9 and 9, so the weakest is 7% and A($t$) holds for $t < 7$: the largest whole $t$ is 6. Swapping the quantifiers moved the limit from 2 to 6.
